docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: What's up guys, welcome back to CrimeTimeSnacks. On Monday, September 21, 2026, at ten in the morning, three judges of the Indiana Court of Appeals are scheduled to sit in the Supreme Court Courtroom at the Indiana Statehouse. Each side gets thirty minutes. The question in front of them is whether Richard Allen got a fair trial. If you listened to my Delphi episode back in 2022, you know where we left it.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Two girls, a bridge, a few seconds of video, and no arrest. A lot has happened since then. There was an arrest. There was a trial. There was a verdict, and a sentence of 130 years. So let me be clear about where things stand before we start. Richard Allen is not an accused man anymore. A jury convicted him of murdering Abby Williams and Libby German.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: He is also a man with an appeal pending, and he has the right to make it. An appeal is not proof that the jury got it wrong, and it is not proof that they got it right. It is a set of questions. Today I want to walk you through how this case got to a verdict, and then through the three questions his lawyers are asking. Let's unpack it. I am going to keep the recap short, because most of you know it.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: At one thirty in the afternoon on February 13, 2017, Libby German's older sister, Kelsi, dropped two girls off on County Road 300 North, outside Delphi, Indiana. Libby was fourteen. Her friend, Abby Williams, was thirteen. They had the day off from school, and they were going to walk the Monon High Bridge, an abandoned rail bridge over Deer Creek.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: At 2:07, Libby posted a photo of Abby walking the bridge. After that, nobody heard from them again. They were supposed to meet Libby's father at 3:15. They did not show up. The families searched on their own first, and at 5:30 the girls were reported missing. Around noon the next day, Valentine's Day, their bodies were found on the north bank of Deer Creek.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: What made this case different from the start was Libby's phone. When a man came up behind them on that bridge, she started recording. Two days after the murders, Indiana State Police were already circulating a grainy still image of a man walking the rail bridge, hands in his pockets, head down. People started calling him Bridge Guy. On February 22, police released a piece of audio from the same phone.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: It is a man's voice, muffled, saying three words. Down the hill. Police called Libby a hero for having the presence of mind to record it. They also said there was more on the phone, and that they were holding it back so they would not compromise a future trial. At that point the reward stood at 41,000 dollars. Then the years went by. A composite sketch came out that July.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: In April 2019, State Police announced what they called a new direction and released a second sketch. They told the public the killer might be hiding in plain sight, and that he was almost certainly familiar with Delphi, from living there, working there, or some other reason. They were right about that. They just did not know they already had his name.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: In that same 2019 announcement, police asked for help with one more thing. They wanted to identify the driver of a vehicle that had been left at the former Child Services office, just off the Hoosier Heartland Highway, between noon and five on the day of the murders. Over the years, investigators ran down thousands of leads. None of them ended in an arrest.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Three days after the murders, a man walked up to an Indiana conservation officer who was helping on the case. They talked in a grocery store parking lot. The man said he had been on the trails the afternoon the girls disappeared, and that he had passed three girls along the way. His name was Richard Allen. The officer typed up his notes and turned them in.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: And then the paperwork went nowhere. Allen's last name was recorded incorrectly on the tip, and the file was marked cleared. It sat like that for five years. In September 2022, a volunteer file clerk named Kathy Shank was helping investigators organize thousands of old tips. She found the conservation officer's notes, worked out that the tip was about Richard Allen, and brought it to the investigator on the case.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: At trial, Carroll County Sheriff Tony Liggett put it this way. The tip fell in the cracks, he said, and Allen was hiding in plain sight. Things moved fast after that. On October 13, 2022, police interviewed Allen again. He told them he had worn jeans and a black or blue jacket that day, and that he had gone out to the bridge to watch fish.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Police searched his home and recovered a pistol. Remember that pistol, because it becomes the center of the physical case. On October 26, 2022, Richard Allen was taken into custody. On October 31, State Police announced he had been charged with two counts of murder. He pleaded not guilty. Time magazine called it the first major break in a case that had captivated national attention for nearly six years.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: A month later, Judge Frances Gull unsealed the probable cause affidavit, with redactions. According to that document, the video from Libby's phone showed one of the girls mentioning a gun as a man in a dark jacket and jeans approached and ordered them down the hill. Investigators had found an unspent forty caliber round less than two feet from one of the bodies, between the two girls.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: One witness described a man walking away from the bridge in a blue jacket and blue jeans, muddy and bloody. Another described a car parked oddly, as if to hide its license plate. Investigators said the description matched a car Allen owned in 2017. So who was he? Richard Matthew Allen was born in September 1972 and grew up in Mexico, Indiana.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: He played football and ran track in high school, graduated in 1991, studied accounting at a community college, and had short stints in the Army and the National Guard. He married and had one daughter. From 2003 to 2013 he managed a Walmart in Logansport. In December 2006 he moved to Delphi. After Walmart, he went to work for CVS, and he got his pharmacy technician license in February 2018.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: That is one year after the murders. Delphi is a town of about 3,000 people. One resident told A&E that he was a familiar face if you went into the CVS. And there is one detail that people in town could not get past after the arrest. Libby's grandmother, Becky Patty, told reporters that Allen had printed photos of the two girls, at no charge, for their funerals.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Years later, in court, she said it this way. He developed photos with no remorse, and he didn't blink. Allen never hid the fact that he was out there. Shortly after the murders he told his wife he had been on the trail that day. After his arrest, he told investigators he had been at his mother's house in Peru, Indiana, that morning, got to the trail around midday, saw three girls pass by, saw nobody else, and watched

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: His defense would later point at all of this. He lived in Delphi for more than five years after the killings. He went to police on his own. The prosecution pointed at the same facts and saw something else: a man who put himself on that trail at the time the girls disappeared. The trial was originally set for March 20, 2023. It did not start until October 2024, and the road in between was rough.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: In December 2022, Judge Gull put a gag order on the case. The defense asked to move the trial out of Carroll County, arguing that the extensive media attention made a fair local jury impossible. Two public defenders, Brad Rozzi and Andrew Baldwin, were appointed to represent Allen, and the first trial date was pushed back so they could get through the discovery.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Then, in October 2023, crime scene photos leaked from the defense team's office. Judge Gull removed both attorneys from the case, citing gross negligence. The attorneys took that to the Indiana Supreme Court, and the justices reinstated them. Those photos never went away, either. After sentencing, the prosecutor said they were still out there, and he asked anyone who receives them to delete them rather than put the f

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: The other fight was over what the defense wanted to argue. Allen's lawyers suggested the girls were killed as part of a pagan ritual sacrifice, by followers of Odinism, a Norse pagan religion. They accused police of ignoring evidence from the crime scene, and they pointed to a search warrant request from March 2017 in which an FBI agent said the bodies appeared to have been moved and staged.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Judge Gull repeatedly rejected motions to bring that theory in front of the jury. Hold on to that ruling. It is one of the three things the Court of Appeals is being asked about. While all of that was going on, Richard Allen was not sitting in a county jail. He was being held at Westville Correctional Facility, a state prison, and his lawyers say he spent thirteen months in solitary confinement before he got his day

docs.text: Here is what the jury heard about that time. Monica Wala was the lead psychologist at Westville. She testified that Allen first told her he was innocent. In April 2023, around the time he was put back on suicide watch, that changed. He was on suicide watch twice. According to her testimony, he showed bizarre behavior, including eating his own feces and banging his head, and at one point he was diagnosed with a brief

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: And he started confessing. On April 3, 2023, on a recorded call to his wife, Kathy, he said, I killed Abby and Libby. When she pushed back, he said, I think I did. I don't know. I wish they would kill me and let me apologize to the families. On a call with his mother the following month he said, I'm just worried you guys aren't going to love me because I said I did it.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Wala testified that Allen told her, I killed Abby and Libby. I'm sorry. She said he told her he had originally planned to sexually assault the girls, that he ran when he saw a van nearby, and that he cut their throats and covered their bodies with sticks. Prosecutors counted more than sixty of these statements. To his wife. To his mother. To the psychologist, the warden, other prison employees, and other inmates.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: In person, on the phone, and in writing. The defense called Deanna Dwenger, a clinical psychologist who worked for the Department of Correction's behavioral health service. She testified that in April 2023, the same month the confessions began, Allen was diagnosed with a serious mental illness, and that a team of mental health professionals concluded he had a grave disability.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: A neuropsychologist hired by the defense testified to pretty severe depression. So both sides agree that he said it. What they disagree about is what state he was in when he said it, and whose fault that was. That is the second question in the appeal. The trial began on October 18, 2024, in Delphi, in front of a sequestered jury of seven women and five men.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: There were seventeen days of testimony. People were so desperate to get in that, according to one resident, podcasters and YouTubers were paying people to sit in lawn chairs overnight to hold their place in line. The first day set the tone. Becky Patty, Libby's grandmother, took the stand and described her last conversation with her granddaughter.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: She had told Libby to take a jacket. Libby answered, Grandma, I'll be OK. Prosecutor Nick McLeland's theory was simple. Richard Allen is Bridge Guy. He forced the girls down the hill at gunpoint, and he killed them. Prosecutors told the jury both girls had their throats cut. Abby was found fully clothed, in Libby's clothing. Libby was found nude.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: The phone was found underneath Abby's body, and McLeland later praised Abby for hiding it from the killer so that police could find it. The state showed jurors a digitally enhanced, 43-second version of Libby's video. State Police Master Trooper Brian Harshman testified that he had listened to more than 700 of Allen's prison phone calls, and that in his opinion the voice of Bridge Guy is the voice of Richard Allen.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Witnesses said they saw a man on the trail that day whose clothes matched the man in the video. Investigators testified that Allen was off work that day and had no alibi. Then the round. A State Police firearms examiner testified that the unspent forty caliber cartridge found between the girls had been cycled through Allen's pistol, a Sig Sauer P226, based on the quality and quantity of the marks on it.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: That was the state's key piece of physical evidence. And the jury heard the confessions, including the phone calls, in Allen's own voice. A journalist who sat through the trial, Susan Hendricks, said he did not sound psychotic or manic on those calls. She said it sounded like a casual conversation. Brad Rozzi's closing argument for the defense came down to three things.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: A broken timeline. False confessions. And no DNA and no weapon. On the physical evidence, the defense had a real point, and the state's own witness made it for them. A DNA expert testifying for the prosecution found none of Allen's DNA at the crime scene. None of Abby's or Libby's DNA was found on anything recovered from his home. The murder weapon was never found.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: On the round, the defense asked why more images had not been taken of the cartridge, and suggested it could have come from a law enforcement officer's weapon. On identification, Rozzi told jurors that no witness clearly identified Allen as the man on the trail or on the bridge that afternoon. And on the confessions, the defense said they were false, the product of months in solitary confinement while his mental healt

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Their argument was that you cannot take the words of a man in that condition and treat them like a calm admission. Rozzi closed with the fact that Allen never left town. He had every chance to run, he told the jury, but he did not, because he didn't do it. Nick McLeland had already walked the jury through the evidence, the photos, the video, and the recorded calls.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: He told them he believed the evidence was firmly convincing that Richard Allen is Bridge Guy, and he killed Abby and Libby. The jury got the case on Thursday, November 7. Before the verdict came in, Judge Gull said something from the bench that turned out to be true. Regardless of what the verdict is, she said, people aren't going to be happy.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: They deliberated for about nineteen hours over three days. On November 11, 2024, they found Richard Allen guilty on all four counts: two counts of murder and two counts of felony murder, for killing each girl while attempting to commit kidnapping. Allen sat without emotion as it was read. Outside the courthouse the crowd broke into applause.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Some people out there were holding signs supporting him. His wife, Kathy, told a reporter on her way out, this isn't over at all. Sentencing was December 20, 2024. The seats reserved for Allen's family were empty. None of his relatives came. Judge Gull gave him sixty-five years for each murder, to be served one after the other, 130 years in total, with credit for the 760 days he had already served.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: The gag order came off that day, and for the first time the families could talk. Becky Patty told the court, I can never change my choice to let Libby and Abby go to the trails that day. Abby's grandmother, Diane Erskin, said she never let herself leave the courtroom, even during the worst testimony, because Abby's last words on the recording were, don't leave me up here.

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: Libby's grandfather, Mike Patty, spoke directly to Allen. You need to stand up, he said, and not appeal. And Judge Gull told him, I've spent 27 years as a judge, and you rank right up there with the most heinous crimes in the state of Indiana. These families, she said, will deal with your carnage forever. State Police Lieutenant Jerry Holeman told the judge the girls had been stalked, kidnapped, humiliated, and treat

docs.title: Delphi: The Appeal
docs.text: He called Allen manipulative and persuasive, and said he showed a lack of remorse. Libby's mother, Carrie Timmons, said Allen's decisions had created a path of destruction. Afterward, Sheriff Liggett apologized to the families for how long it had taken. There will never be any closure in this case, he said. docs.title: Locard's Exchange Principle
docs.text: The foundation of forensic science: every contact between two objects leaves a trace. A perpetrator brings something to a scene and takes something away.

docs.title: Chain of Custody
docs.text: The documented, unbroken record of who handled a piece of evidence, when, and why. A gap can get the evidence excluded at trial.

docs.title: Touch DNA
docs.text: Skin cells transferred by handling an object. Powerful but controversial — a few cells can travel on a handshake and land where their owner never was.

docs.title: CODIS
docs.text: The FBI's Combined DNA Index System, linking DNA profiles across local, state, and national databases.

docs.title: Forensic Genetic Genealogy
docs.text: Identifying suspects by matching crime-scene DNA to distant relatives in public genealogy databases, then building the family tree inward.

docs.title: Mitochondrial DNA
docs.text: DNA inherited only through the maternal line. Survives in degraded remains where nuclear DNA doesn't — common in cold case identifications.

docs.title: DNA Phenotyping
docs.text: Predicting physical traits — ancestry, eye color, hair color — from DNA alone, often used to generate suspect composites.

docs.title: Latent Print
docs.text: A fingerprint invisible to the naked eye, developed with powder, chemicals, or light sources.

docs.title: Ballistics
docs.text: The analysis of firearms, ammunition, and toolmarks — matching a bullet or casing to the weapon that fired it.

docs.title: Gunshot Residue (GSR)
docs.text: Microscopic particles expelled when a firearm is discharged. Presence suggests proximity to a shooting; absence proves little.

docs.title: Luminol
docs.text: A chemical that fluoresces on contact with the iron in hemoglobin, revealing cleaned or invisible bloodstains. It points — it doesn't prove.

docs.title: Bloodstain Pattern Analysis
docs.text: Reading the size, shape, and distribution of bloodstains to reconstruct events. Admissible but heavily contested science.

docs.title: Autopsy
docs.text: The medical examination of a body after death to establish cause and manner of death.

docs.title: Cause of Death
docs.text: The specific injury or disease that ended a life — for example, asphyxiation or a gunshot wound.

docs.title: Manner of Death
docs.text: The classification of how the cause arose: natural, accident, suicide, homicide, or undetermined.

docs.title: Rigor Mortis
docs.text: Post-mortem muscle stiffening, beginning within hours and fully set around twelve — one of several clocks used to estimate time of death.

docs.title: Livor Mortis
docs.text: The settling of blood after death, staining the lowest parts of the body. Fixed lividity can show a body was moved.

docs.title: Forensic Entomology
docs.text: Using insect evidence — species and life stage — to estimate how long a body has been where it was found.

docs.title: Forensic Odontology
docs.text: Dental identification of remains, and the now-discredited practice of bite mark matching.

docs.title: Isotope Analysis
docs.text: Chemistry that reads bones, teeth, and hair to reconstruct where a person lived and what they ate — a tool for identifying unknown remains.

docs.title: Trace Evidence
docs.text: Small transferred materials — fibers, hair, paint, glass, soil — that link people, places, and objects.

docs.title: Exemplar
docs.text: A known sample — handwriting, DNA, prints — collected from a person for comparison against evidence.

docs.title: Cold Hit
docs.text: A database match that identifies a suspect with no prior connection to the investigation.

docs.title: Person of Interest
docs.text: Someone investigators want to talk to. Not an accusation — a step below suspect.

docs.title: Suspect
docs.text: A person investigators believe may have committed the crime, based on evidence.

docs.title: Modus Operandi (M.O.)
docs.text: An offender's method of committing crime — learned behavior that can evolve over time.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text: What an offender does beyond what's necessary to commit the crime — the psychological fingerprint that stays constant while an M.O. changes.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text: Deliberately altering a crime scene to mislead investigators — making a homicide look like a burglary gone wrong, for instance.

docs.title: Victimology
docs.text: The study of the victim — routines, relationships, risk factors — to understand why they were targeted and by whom.

docs.title: Canvass
docs.text: Systematic door-to-door interviews around a crime scene, hunting for witnesses and cameras.

docs.title: BOLO
docs.text: 'Be on the lookout' — an alert to law enforcement describing a person or vehicle of interest.

docs.title: AMBER Alert
docs.text: The public emergency alert for abducted children in credible, imminent danger — named for Amber Hagerman.

docs.title: NamUs
docs.text: The National Missing and Unidentified Persons System — the public database that matches missing persons cases to unidentified remains.

docs.title: ViCAP
docs.text: The FBI's Violent Criminal Apprehension Program, linking violent crimes across jurisdictions by behavioral and physical details.

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text: Inferring offender characteristics from crime scene behavior. A lead-generating tool, not evidence.

docs.title: The First 48
docs.text: The investigative truism that solve rates drop sharply after the first two days — evidence degrades, memories fade, trails cool.

docs.title: Cold Case
docs.text: An unsolved case no longer under active investigation, kept open pending new leads or technology.

docs.title: Exhumation
docs.text: The court-ordered removal of buried remains for new examination.

docs.title: Jurisdiction
docs.text: Which agency owns a case — a frequent source of friction and, in serial cases, missed connections.

docs.title: Task Force
docs.text: A multi-agency team assembled for one investigation, pooling jurisdiction and resources.

docs.title: Tip Line
docs.text: The public's channel into an investigation. High noise, occasionally the whole case.

docs.title: Geofence Warrant
docs.text: A court order for data on every device inside an area during a time window — powerful and constitutionally contested.

docs.title: Cell Tower Ping
docs.text: A phone's contact with a tower, placing it in a general area — not a precise location, whatever TV says.

docs.title: Probable Cause
docs.text: The legal threshold for arrests and warrants: enough facts for a reasonable person to believe a crime occurred.

docs.title: Miranda Rights
docs.text: The warnings required before custodial interrogation — silence and counsel. Unwarned statements risk suppression.

docs.title: Indictment
docs.text: A grand jury's formal accusation, moving a case toward trial.

docs.title: Grand Jury
docs.text: Citizens who review the prosecution's evidence in secret and decide whether charges proceed. They indict; they don't convict.

docs.title: Arraignment
docs.text: The first court appearance: charges read, plea entered, bail argued.

docs.title: Plea Bargain
docs.text: Resolving a case by agreement — a plea in exchange for reduced charges or sentence. How most criminal cases actually end.

docs.title: Alford Plea
docs.text: A guilty plea in which the defendant maintains innocence while conceding the evidence would convict.

docs.title: No Contest (Nolo Contendere)
docs.text: Accepting conviction without admitting guilt — often to limit exposure in a civil suit.

docs.title: Beyond a Reasonable Doubt
docs.text: The criminal standard of proof — the highest in the legal system.

docs.title: Circumstantial Evidence
docs.text: Evidence requiring an inference — fully legitimate, routinely conviction-grade, and routinely misunderstood.

docs.title: Direct Evidence
docs.text: Evidence that proves a fact without inference — an eyewitness, a confession, a recording.

docs.title: Hearsay
docs.text: An out-of-court statement offered for its truth. Generally inadmissible, with a long list of exceptions.

docs.title: Exculpatory Evidence
docs.text: Evidence favorable to the defendant. Prosecutors must disclose it — that's Brady.

docs.title: Brady Violation
docs.text: The state's failure to turn over exculpatory evidence — grounds for reversal.

docs.title: Double Jeopardy
docs.text: The constitutional bar on retrying an acquitted defendant for the same offense.

docs.title: Statute of Limitations
docs.text: The deadline for filing charges. Murder almost never has one.

docs.title: Change of Venue
docs.text: Moving a trial when local publicity makes a fair jury impossible.

docs.title: Voir Dire
docs.text: Jury selection — the questioning that surfaces bias before a juror is seated.

docs.title: Sequestration
docs.text: Isolating a jury from outside information during trial or deliberation.

docs.title: Hung Jury
docs.text: A jury that cannot reach unanimity, ending in mistrial. The state may retry.

docs.title: Mistrial
docs.text: A trial terminated without verdict — for a hung jury, misconduct, or prejudicial error.

docs.title: Acquittal
docs.text: A not-guilty verdict. Not a declaration of innocence — a finding that proof fell short.

docs.title: Exoneration
docs.text: The formal clearing of a convicted person, often years later, by new evidence.

docs.title: Habeas Corpus
docs.text: The post-conviction challenge to unlawful detention — the vehicle for many innocence claims.

docs.title: Life Without Parole (LWOP)
docs.text: A life sentence with no possibility of release — in practice, the alternative to capital punishment.

docs.title: Insanity Defense
docs.text: The claim that mental disease prevented understanding the act or its wrongfulness. Rarely raised, more rarely successful.

docs.title: Competency to Stand Trial
docs.text: Whether a defendant can understand proceedings and assist counsel now — a different question from insanity at the time of the offense.

docs.title: Extradition
docs.text: The formal transfer of a suspect between states or countries — and why some fugitives choose their refuge carefully.

docs.title: Jailhouse Informant
docs.text: An incarcerated witness trading testimony for benefit. A leading cause of wrongful convictions.

docs.title: Wrongful Conviction
docs.text: A conviction of the innocent — driven by misidentification, false confession, flawed forensics, and misconduct.

docs.title: False Confession
docs.text: An innocent person's admission of guilt — produced by coercion, exhaustion, youth, or suggestion. It happens far more than intuition allows.
